title: 3-Read Friday #43: Mistakes, Ofsted, and Effective CPD
author: Craig Barton
summary: Barton's final 3-Read Friday before the summer break moves from classroom culture out to whole-school and system-level concerns. He opens with Jo Castelino's practical suggestions for building a genuine culture of error, framing the challenge as reconciling the ideal of a mistake-friendly classroom with how genuinely painful it can feel for a child to be wrong in front of peers. He then turns to Peter Foster's synthesis of 70 Ofsted reports, singling out Foster's finding that Checking for Understanding sits at the top of what Good-rated secondary schools are told to improve. He closes by breaking his usual blog-only format to recommend Ollie Lovell's podcast interview with Harry Fletcher-Wood on running effective professional development, calling it essential listening for anyone who leads CPD or department meetings.
points: Barton frames the culture-of-error challenge as a tension between the theoretical ideal and the real social cost of being wrong in front of classmates.
He highlights Foster's specific finding, drawn from 70 Ofsted reports, that Checking for Understanding was the top improvement area for Good-rated secondary schools.
He deliberately breaks his usual link format to recommend an audio interview, signalling how highly he rates it for anyone responsible for running CPD.
The issue closes out before summer by pivoting from classroom-level culture to school- and system-level improvement priorities.
quotes: Every teacher wants a classroom where their students are not afraid to make mistakes - a culture of error is the fancy term for this.
But how do we create such a culture when making a mistake in front of your peers can be one of the worst feelings in the world for a child?
Pete has read 70 Ofsted reports in an effort to pick out the key things schools - according to Ofsted, at least - should look to improve.
I found the section on what secondary schools rated as Good should work on, with Checking for Understanding right at the top of the list.
I am going rogue for my final entry by recommending a podcast.
Ollie's interview with Harry Fletcher-Wood is absolute gold for anyone who plans or runs CPD, whether senior leaders, or heads of department leading meetings.
